kp.k: Katyal reports AI-assisted Supreme Court argument preparation
kp.d: In his quoted tweet, Katyal describes working over the preceding year with Harvey, the legal-AI company, on a bespoke system trained on 25 years of Justices’ oral-argument questions and their writings. He claims it anticipated many questions, sometimes nearly verbatim, in the tariffs case his team won 6-3. This is a practitioner’s account of preparation support, not a measured evaluation or evidence establishing AI’s contribution to the outcome. A May 12 update reports Sarah Isgur questioning Harvey’s performance and identifying apparent discrepancies between Katyal’s account and the argument transcript.
qs: Harvey predicted many of the questions the Justices asked—sometimes almost word for word.
Harvey is a bespoke AI I built over the last year with a legal AI company, trained on every question every Justice has asked in oral argument for 25 years, and everything they've ever written.

Sarah Isgur questioned whether Harvey was really as great at Katyal claimed—and found some apparent discrepancies between Katyal’s account of certain portions of the argument and the [transcript](https://www.supremecourt.gov/oral_arguments/argument_transcripts/2025/24-1287_b07d.pdf).

kp.k: Katyal locates lawyers’ advantage in human connection
kp.d: Katyal frames AI as an analytical and predictive preparation aid rather than a substitute for the advocate. He attributes the decisive contribution to reading the courtroom and responding to a Justice’s underlying concern, recommending that professionals deepen this purportedly irreducible human skill. The claim about what won the case is his interpretation, not an established causal finding.
qs: AI can predict. AI can analyze. What AI cannot do is the one thing that actually won the argument.
Connect. Read the room. Hear not just a Justice's words, but her worry—and answer the worry.
That is the irreducibly human skill.
Find yours. Go deeper. In this age of AI, that's where your edge lives.

kp.k: Critics dispute the victory narrative and individual credit
kp.d: Lat reports criticism that Katyal overstated both his personal contribution and the difficulty of winning, complicating the narrative linking AI and coaching to litigation success. Dan Epps argues the four coaches had no effect; Lat says most commentators he followed expected an administration defeat. Lat qualifies his selection of largely negative reactions as idiosyncratic and drawn mainly from X, and a later update acknowledges largely positive LinkedIn assessments. These are competing interpretations and reactions, not evidence measuring advocacy or AI effectiveness.
qs: Counterpoint: the Justices are good at figuring out what they think about a case of this magnitude, and Neal’s four coaches had zero effect on the outcome.
I don’t think I have ever seen a SCOTUS advocate claim so much personal credit for a win before
Most commentators, myself included, viewed the tariffs case as a likely defeat for the administration
Reactions to Katyal’s tweet and TED Talk were not universally negative.

kp.k: Katyal advocates multidisciplinary teams and practice-oriented learning
kp.d: In his response to Lat, Katyal says the talk was intended to acknowledge vulnerability and explain how practitioners develop through teams, including experts outside law. He places AI within that broader learning model and urges lawyers to find practical tools that translate law-school theory into practice. His own account includes mindset, improvisation and meditation coaches alongside Harvey; it does not propose a staffing structure or quantify training benefits.
qs: The idea of the talk is to encourage people to find the tools in practice to do what law school teaches in theory.
The one skill I feel confident of today is the ability to put together fabulous teams and learn from them.
For lawyers specifically, a winning team may very well turn out to include non-lawyers you can learn from, too.
The AI piece is part of that.

kp.k: Katyal predicts fundamental professional change and judicial adoption
kp.d: Katyal predicts a seismic shift in legal practice, describing his Supreme Court preparation as only an early indication of AI’s future significance. He asks how current law students will practise in 5, 15 and 50 years, asserts that lawyers already use AI, and predicts judges will soon do so if they do not already. He recommends immediate professional discussion rather than denial. These are broad forecasts without adoption statistics or specified mechanisms for changing employment, pricing or firm structure.
qs: Our profession is on the verge of a seismic shift, and the legal profession doesn’t understand what is about to happen.
What we did with AI is just the tip of the iceberg, and we need to begin talking about it.
ChatGPT is only a couple of years old—how will the folks going to law school today be practicing in 5, 15, and 50 years?
Lawyers are already using AI, soon judges will be (if they aren’t already), and we need to begin that conversation now, and the Talk is an attempt to do that.

kp.k: Harvey endorsement prompts questions about material connections
kp.d: Lat asks whether Katyal’s praise of Harvey required disclosure of a material connection under FTC influencer requirements, including whether free or discounted access might constitute a benefit. Katyal denies a financial relationship, discounts or incentives and says his organisation pays on ordinary customer terms. Lat also quotes a Harvey spokesperson denying a promotional arrangement or equity stake. The article raises endorsement transparency but does not establish a disclosure violation.
qs: “I have no financial relationship with Harvey,” he told me. “I worked with their engineers for free.”
“I received no discount or other incentives,” Katyal said. “We are paying customers, and I used it on same terms as everyone else.”
has no arrangement with Katyal to promote its services, and he doesn’t hold any investment or equity stake in the company.

kp.k: Lat challenges emotional intelligence as an exclusively human advantage
kp.d: Lat rejects Katyal’s categorical claim that AI cannot navigate human emotions, using a personal, nonlegal communication example. He reports that ChatGPT identified his draft response to a teacher as panicky and defensive and supplied a calmer alternative, which he and his husband preferred, reviewed and edited before sending. This is anecdotal analogy evidence about communication assistance and human verification, not a finding about courtroom advocacy or general AI emotional competence.
qs: And I actually don’t buy the argument that AI can’t navigate human emotions.
ChatGPT helpfully provided me with an alternative response that was far more calm and measured.
So he and I carefully reviewed and edited the ChatGPT draft
It went over well, we subsequently had a productive meeting with her, and everything is fine now—thanks in part to the high EQ of ChatGPT.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Katyal describes AI-assisted Supreme Court preparation, predicts fundamental changes to legal practice, and identifies human connection as the advocate’s remaining edge; Lat disputes the categorical exclusion of AI from emotional understanding.
pts.d: Neal Katyal claims that a bespoke system developed with Harvey’s engineers anticipated Supreme Court questions, sometimes almost verbatim. He frames AI as augmenting advocates’ preparation and analysis rather than replacing the advocate: he attributes the decisive contribution to human connection and reading the Justices’ concerns. In his interview with Lat, Katyal predicts a seismic professional shift, fundamentally different practice for current law students, and judicial adoption of AI. David Lat endorses engaging with AI rather than ignoring it, but challenges Katyal’s assertion that AI cannot navigate human emotions. Lat’s supporting example concerns personal correspondence, not legal advocacy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is personal experience: Katyal’s account of one Supreme Court preparation effort and Lat’s account of ChatGPT improving an emotionally sensitive email.
pts.d: Katyal describes a year of development with a legal-AI company and training on 25 years of Justices’ oral-argument questions and their writings. His report of predicted questions and the 6–3 victory is an experiential account, not a benchmark or a measurement isolating AI’s contribution to the outcome. The article reports challenges to his narrative, but supplies no systematic performance evaluation. Katyal extrapolates from this experience to profession-wide transformation without offering adoption data or quantified forecasts. Lat supports his disagreement about emotional understanding with a personal anecdote: ChatGPT identified his draft response to a teacher as an overreaction and produced a calmer alternative, which he and his husband reviewed and edited before sending. The quoted AI-generated parody is satire, not evidence of Harvey’s capabilities. On the commercial context of Katyal’s endorsement, Katyal says he received no financial benefit or preferential access; the article also reports corroboration from Harvey.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Katyal distinguishes already-demonstrated preparation assistance from imminent judicial adoption and longer-term professional transformation.
pts.d: Writing in May 2026, the article reproduces Katyal’s account of arguing the case five months earlier and building the bespoke AI over the preceding year. Its reported preparation capability is tied to that system and its judicial-record training material, not established for all AI tools. Katyal describes lawyer adoption as already occurring, judicial adoption as coming soon or possibly already occurring, and broader transformation as unfolding over the years ahead. He raises 5-, 15-, and 50-year horizons for current law students without specifying what practice will look like at each interval. His human-edge claim is categorical in wording, not given an explicit expiry date. Lat’s contrasting emotional-understanding example occurred earlier in 2026 and involved human review and editing before use.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate application concerns Supreme Court advocates; the forecast extends to lawyers generally, judges, and current law students.
pts.d: Katyal presents AI as a preparation resource for high-level litigators and their teams, helping anticipate judicial questioning. He urges lawyers to develop interpersonal skills as a source of differentiation alongside AI’s predictive and analytical capabilities. His broader forecast concerns the legal profession and the future practice of current law students, with judges identified as prospective or existing users but no specific judicial workflow described. Small-business clients appear in the underlying litigation, but the article does not separately claim that AI improved their access to justice or reduced their fees. It offers no concrete predictions about staffing, lawyer displacement, pricing, or legal-market shares. Lat’s emotional-understanding anecdote concerns parents communicating with a teacher and does not itself establish a legal-services application.
